idiom_name: abstract Authenticator interface + factory registry of std::function creators (C++11)
implementation_notes: Hand-written structure: an abstract class with a pure virtual authenticate(credentials) returning std::shared_ptr<Principal> (available in C++11) or a Result type, one concrete class per mechanism (password, X.509, JWT), and a registry mapping configured names to factories (std::unordered_map<std::string, std::function<std::unique_ptr<Authenticator>()>>). The standard library never verifies identities, so the payoff is entirely the seam: mechanism-specific cryptography (OpenSSL, libsodium, a JWT library) stays inside the concrete authenticator and callers see only the principal. On C++20 toolchains the same seam can be expressed as an awaitable interface so network-backed verification suspends instead of blocking.
pitfalls: A virtual destructor is mandatory; deleting a concrete authenticator through the base pointer otherwise leaks it.

Constructing an authenticator (and its crypto context or JWKS cache) per request is expensive -> a factory can discard reusable verification state -> cache immutable context or return a shared long-lived instance while keeping per-request state local.

Throwing from authenticate() erases the difference between invalid credentials and verifier failure -> callers cannot choose safe 401 versus outage handling -> return a Result type with explicit error categories and reserve exceptions for programming errors.
Certificate and key material must be owned by value (smart pointers), never referenced from a request-scoped buffer that dies first.

variants.name: Awaitable Authenticator on C++20 coroutines
variants.idiom_name: co_await authenticator.authenticate(credentials) on an event-loop executor
variants.implementation_notes: Network-backed mechanisms (directory bind, OIDC discovery and JWKS fetch, revocation check) block a thread in the classic shape; C++20 stackless coroutines let the same one-operation interface become awaitable, so a single event loop serves many concurrent verifications. The seam does not change - still one operation yielding a principal - but the return type becomes a task/awaitable and the implementation must keep its state alive across suspension. Choose it when verification is I/O-bound and the toolchain has C++20 coroutines.
pitfalls: State captured in a coroutine frame must outlive every suspension; a reference to a request-scoped credential is the coroutine-era dangling-pointer bug.
Blocking calls (DNS, file I/O, synchronous crypto) inside an awaitable silently stall the whole executor.
Detached tasks that outlive the request must not touch the connection or request object they started from.
